utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, you said that you found an invitation card in front of you on your table in your office, inviting you to attend this meeting. So there was an invitation without a name; is that it? Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. My name was not specified. No name specification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, so it was an anonymous invitation, an invitation "To whom it may concern," not to any specific person by name.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: The invitation was sent to the president of the assembly. But the name and the surname wasn't specified. It said "The president of the assembly." So in this case, and in similar cases, if the president of the assembly was not available, he would have his deputy, and the deputy would be a volunteer. He would say "I'll go instead." Or if I receive an invitation as president of the Executive Board and I am not there, then the deputy president of the assembly would go to the meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the invitation was addressed to the president in actual fact?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now, what reception were you given once you entered, when you got there, when you arrived at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, nobody actually received me. Nobody noticed me. Nobody made a note of my being there, nor did anybody ask me anything, just like the others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So who led the reception? Who was the main person there?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know. I didn't even make an effort to see who was chairing the reception. There were several speakers, and I think, but I repeat I think, I don't think there was a chairman. There wasn't any one specific person who chaired the meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And do you remember who the organisers were, if I can put it that way, of that meeting? Was it organised by the SDS party, or were there functionaries, party officials there, from the administration, for example? Do you happen to remember?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's like this, you see: A lot of time has gone by since then. I said that the meeting was attended mostly by the presidents of assemblies and the presidents of the executive boards of the 17 municipalities, with the exception, I think I said that, with the exception of the president of the assembly of Prijedor. He was not invited because he was the only Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But they were all of Serb ethnicity, were they? They were all Serbs then?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of them, yes. And I assumed -- I assumed they were all Serbs because there were just two of us Bosniaks, but nobody attached any importance to us, nobody contacted us, came up to us to speak to us or anything like that. Although I must say we didn't know these people very well because they were people who had been elected at the elections of the year 2000, so they came into office as of January 2001, so we didn't have a chance of getting to know them beforehand. We didn't actually know all these people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But to your knowledge, this particular meeting, do you think it was convened by the party authorities or the administrative authorities, or who?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both, I assume. Both the party and state authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you base your assumptions on what? How do you come to that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because it was a one-ethnicity meeting. Uni-national.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But you said that it was convened by the party authorities, the SDS party that means, and also by the administrative sections as well. Governmental, if I can put it that way, the governmental authorities and strata.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I assume that that's how it was, although there wasn't a joint organ for Bosnian Krajina at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you confirm, you do confirm and assert that no high dignitaries either from the party or the government were present. They were just the presidents of the municipalities. Right? Local level?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said I assumed they were the presidents of the municipalities where the Serbs were presidents, presidents of the executive boards where it was a Serb president again, and the party of representatives as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you left with the impression that it was more a meeting which had received instructions, or was it a debate, an open debate and discussion amongst the participants? Did it give an opportunity of all the people present to express their own opinions, or were they following some instructions and guidelines? I don't know whether I'm making myself clear enough. What I'm saying is this: Was it more a meeting which had as its goal the discussion of certain questions pursuant to instructions and guidelines coming from some quarter, or was it a free debate, an open and frank discussion and debate amongst the participants, the presidents of the municipalities, as you said, who were freely expressing their opinions, their individual opinions?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, it was a sort of underhand debate. I never said that before, but I do remember that there were two people who had the main say in Banja Luka. It was Professor Mico Carevic and Kugo Lazarevic. I know that these two men had the main say, and they would steer the people taking part in the discussion along these lines. And that is what I said that the president of the court for misdemeanors from Srbac, that he said where the funds would be directed and that the Ustashas' and balijas' media should be stifled and that the Serb media should be encouraged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So what about Professor Mico? What was his occupation?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I knew Professor Mico by sight. He was professor at the faculty of law. That's all I know. And I know this other one, Kugo Lazarevic, because I'd seen him around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Both of them were members of the SDS party, were they?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I really don't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But at least Professor Mico was not a municipal president, was he? He wasn't president of a Municipal Assembly, for example, was he, this Professor Mico?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nor the other gentleman?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So now you remember that these two individuals played the role of organisers, if I can put it. They led the debate, they steered the debate.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, they did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And at the end of the meeting, were any decisions made or recommendations adopted?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you, we weren't interested in that because we didn't expect anything like that to take place at the meeting. We even wanted to leave during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But at the end of the meeting, did it end by drafting any recommendations or anything like that? Instructions? Guidelines? Anything particular like that?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I really don't know. All I can tell you is this: I have at home, because I did keep notes but I haven't brought them with me, I haven't brought any documents, but I can, of course, send my notes to the Tribunal, my own diary, my own agenda which has a note of my having attended that meeting, my original notes, the ones I took.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did they decide to meet again at some point in the future, in the near future or the distant future?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I just add, you know when you arrive at a meeting when you expect something nice to happen and then you hear ugly things being said, then you lose interest. You're not interested in taking part. And then you say to myself, What in the world brought me here in the first place? And that's what I and Mr. Draganovic, president of the Executive Board of the Kljuc municipality, discussed amongst ourselves. We thought, Why did we ever come to the meeting in the first place?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you had the possibility to react and explain your point of view, express your point of view, or was that out of the question? Were you not able to take the floor?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you don't realise the kind of times they were and the situation we were in. No, my answer is no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But did you try, at least? Did you try to do anything like that, at least?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I didn't even try. Because it would have ended badly for me had I tried.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I've got a few questions for you as well. You just spoke about your personal notes. Did you make these notes at the time of the events you refer to in these notes?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at the time of the events. That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did you ever discuss the content of your notes with the investigators --

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. No, I didn't, never.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's not much of that. I just recorded that I attended such-and-such a meeting. Made a note of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you offered to make them available for the Chamber if we would like to see them.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, I did offer. The original notes, the whole agenda or notebook.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Judges will consider whether we'll ask you to provide those notes. When you were asked about the list of names you had that those who were interrogating you after your arrest were interested in, you said it doesn't come into my mind at this moment what this refers to. Having had Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. some time perhaps to reflect, is it coming back in your mind what this list of names you spoke about would have been?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I quite understood you. What list are you referring to? What list of names?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In paragraph 35 of your statement - Ms. Loukas has taken you to that paragraph - it reads: "I had a list of names, and they were very interested in. During questioning, the interrogators told Kurbegovic that the secretary of the SDA in Celinac had been arrested. He had documents showing plans for destruction of bridges and that he would tell all." But this paragraph starts with you being in possession of a list of names. Do you remember what that list was about?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It was in the month of March 1992 when I returned from a business trip to Sarajevo. And I have it. I have some of the names. They searched me, took everything out of my pockets, found a list of five names which I had. It was a list I worked with, of the people I worked with, and nothing else. So if you do that to me now, if you take things out of my pocket, you would find lists of names in my pockets, on me. So they searched me. They took everything out of my pockets, everything I had in my pockets, and they saw this list. And this was when I was on a business trip and we were detained for four hours and questioned. It wasn't when I was arrested on the 25th of May. This took place on another occasion, two months before the 25th of May, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I made a mistake. I said after you were arrested. But once you were stopped at the --

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They finally got that list, and this was a list of, I would say business, people you knew from the business you were in?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. Then you explained to us that the president of the Executive Board of the Municipal Assembly or of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor would not have been invited to the meeting in Banja Luka because he was, as you told us, he was a Bosniak. Nevertheless, you and the president of the assembly or of the Executive Board of the Assembly of Kljuc were invited. So out of three non-Serb presidents, two received an invitation, or at least showed up at this meeting where one, you said, was not invited because he was a Bosniak. Could you explain to us how it could be possible that if for reasons of being a Bosniak you would not be invited, that nevertheless two out of three were invited?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is how it was: Muhamed Cehajic was not the president of the Executive Board of Prijedor; he was president of the assembly. And all the presidents of the assemblies of the 17 municipalities were invited, so the invitation that I received was handed over and it read to the president of the Municipal Assembly of Sanski Most. And that was Rasula. So he was invited. And then somebody placed on my table as president of the Executive Board, when I came into my office in the morning, I found this invitation on my table. And I thought well, the president of the assembly was not there, and that was normal, and I as the president of the Executive Board went to the meeting. Had I talked to Mr. Asim Egeric, who also held the same post, he was also president of the Executive Board, whereas he was a Serb, I think from his name, he was president of the assembly and the same thing happened to him. So he said, here is the invitation, and it reads president of the Municipal Assembly of Kljuc, and I came as president of the Executive Board. So we weren't directly invited. It was just by chance that we happened to receive these invitations and attend the meeting. But when I discussed this with the late Mr. Muhamed Cehajic several days later, who was president of the assembly of Prijedor, who belonged to the region, I asked, Why didn't you attend the meeting? And he said, Well, I never receive an invitation to attend at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So now I do understand that more or less by chance you took over the invitation which was not directly addressed to you and would not have been addressed to you as --

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That's quite right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I now understand better.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: And we wouldn't have gone had on that day the president of the assembly, Nedeljko Rasula, been at the office, I wouldn't have gone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear to me. You told us that you testified in a, what I understood, a case against Mr. Draganovic of which we have no further details. Could you tell us, did you testify in open court or did you give a statement? When was it, and could you briefly explain to you us under what circumstances you testified.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is how it was: I was the minister of the Sanski canton for jurisprudence and administration at the time when Mr. Draganovic was the president of the court. And as the minister, in agreement with the finance minister of the day, I had agreed that resources be allocated for the work of the court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're now talking about -- the case. I asked you about whether you testified in open court, whether it was a closed session, whether --

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's right, in open court. In open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In open court. In the presence of Mr. Draganovic? In the presence of --

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was Mr. Draganovic assisted by counsel?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was. I don't know. I think he did have counsel, yes. But I didn't pay attention to that. I think he did. Because nobody asked me any questions when I testified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No one asked you questions when you testified? Not even the court?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't. They didn't ask questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I would like to know what do you mean by testifying? Did you give a -- well, a statement on your own, or -- no questions were put to you?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Before that, I made a written -- gave a written statement. I did give a written statement beforehand. And then I said that I would respond when called about the statement which I signed, and I said I stood by what I had said in my written statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear. You confirmed your written statement you gave earlier.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. The one I gave earlier, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To whom did you give the written statement? To investigators or to a prosecutor or to what kind of a person?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave the written statement to, I think it was the investigating judge at the time. Pursuant to our rules and regulations, statements of that kind would be given to the investigating judge. So I think that's who it was to. Either to the prosecutor or the investigating judge, but I think it was to the judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the presence of the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: The statement in the presence of the defence? No. I gave it of my own free will, I wrote it, signed it, and sent it. And I said that I would be ready to come to court to make my statement with respect to the written statement I had already given if the need arose. I said I confirmed everything I said in the statement, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, regarding that, I think a summary or that statement itself is part of the Rule 68 materials that Defence counsel and I agreed on to submit to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To make it not a secret, what I was seeking to find out is whether your answer that you didn't know that Mr. Draganovic had counsel, whether the circumstances would have given you a clue that he would be assisted by counsel. But the matter has been sufficiently clarified for me. Then my next question would be, are you familiar with the layout of the hall of the Municipal Assembly in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, I wasn't there very often, and I wasn't there after the war. I'd been there before the war on several occasions. So unless anything changed, perhaps I could recognise it. I think I could recognise it as far as the entrance is concerned. Yes, I think I would be able to recognise it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could I ask you to answer a few questions on the basis of the photograph that was presented to you, the photograph I haven't -- could it please be put on the ELMO so that you can have it enlarged on your screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I inquire, does this have a number yet? If not, perhaps we should give it one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't think it has a number yet. But since some other documents have no numbers yet either, I would -- I see you have it. Could you, Madam Registrar, please read the numbers in of all the documents on the list of documents to be used in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I've pre-numbered these already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We'll start with number 1, the ICTY statement. That will be marked D12. Number 2, which is also the ICTY statement but in B/C/S is marked D12/1. Point 3, typewritten information, sheet number 011/92 is marked D13.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm a bit confused by number 3 and 4, but perhaps we should ask for clarification because we find two English versions.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Your Honour. My case manager has just pointed out to me that number 4 is the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Number 4 is the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: So number 4 is the B/C/S version, and it is D13.1. The document, Agreement on the Formation of a Community of Bosnian Krajina Municipalities, is marked as D14.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think as a matter of fact that it should not get a number because it has got already a Prosecution, Exhibit P65, binder 1, tab 27.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: My correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the photograph would be the one which does not appear and would then get number D14, I take it?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D14, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could D14, it is on the ELMO at this moment. Mr. Karabeg, do you recognise the hall or the room where we see a lot of people sitting in?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't think the hall looked like this then. I don't know. I seem to think that it didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you can't help me in that respect. Then I've got one final question to you, or a few questions on the activities you developed in relation to the practice of the JNA in 1991. In your statement, paragraph 19 up until I would say 23 and/or 24, you describe what happened in relation to these practices of the JNA. Do I correctly understand that you found out that you were misinformed about the consent given by the Bosanska Krupa civilian officials for these practices?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was misinformed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And do I also correctly understand your statement to say that you learned that in your absence it was said that you had given your approval for these practices as well?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And do I understand that you learned this from a certain Captain Fuad Kurbegovic?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kurbegovic, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was he a Serb or a non-Serb?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's a Bosniak. His wife is a Serb, so he is in a mixed marriage, but he's a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What information did he tell you about this wrong information provided to others?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: See, it's not that he told me that others had been misinformed. He told me that they had said that I had, too, expressed my consent for these manoeuvres to take place. I did not accept that because they had told me, because this had been accepted the Bosanska Krupa head when I called him to ask him whether he had given his consent for the manoeuvres to take place, he said no one had talked to me about it, nor do I know anything about it. And that's when I said that I could no longer accept it because I had been deluded. They had misinformed me about the consent given by this Bosanska Krupa person. It was then that Kurbegovic said at that meeting that I had given my consent, which was not true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And he told you later, because you did not attend that meeting. And he told you later that this information was given at that meeting where you were absent. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From the whole of your statement, do I understand that you're quite unhappy with these practices where wrong information was given about consent given by civilian authorities and where, as it follows from your statement, Serbs were meeting separately in relation to these JNA activities? Were you unhappy with the situation?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Mostly because they kept meeting amongst themselves, and then only after that, for the sake of appearances, they would talk to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You were asked about what you said in an earlier statement about meeting with non-Serbs to see what you could -- what could be done to protect non-Serbs. On a question of Ms. Loukas, you said that this was a fabrication. I wondered, and perhaps I read it in full in this report of your interview which does not bear a signature, it reads: "1991, practice with JNA. During these practice exercises, there were two teams. The way the JNA practice was how they later launched their attacks in this area. They did the practice in the area of Bosanska Krupa and Kljuc. When Karabeg --" and they are relating to what you had told them. "When Karabeg and others learned about what was happening, they tried to do something about it, so they called and had meeting with non-Serbs who had been serving with the JNA and had reserve ranks in the JNA and now had different occupations to see what could be done to protect non-Serbs." That's what it says. Could you tell us whether you had -- you just told us that you were unhappy with the whole situation, whether you undertook anything and whether you had these kind of meetings to see what could be done about it.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, there were individuals who had accepted this mobilisation under the auspices of the JNA. But when they arrived, it was clear that they were no longer the JNA. The Chetnik cockades were displayed, and various other insignia which indicated that there was only one nation army. And this caused the dissatisfaction amongst the people who then refused to respond to the call-up. So we wanted to see what could be done with respect to that. But we were fearful of the possibility of these people being mobilised and sent to the battlefield in Croatia where they would serve as cannon fodder and give their lives for nothing. It was no longer a JNA; it was a one-nation Serbian army, Chetnik army, wearing typical Chetnik cockades.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand that if you refer to the protection of non-Serbs, that you were concerned rather about what would happen to them if they would be in the army in Croatia or what could happen to non-Serbs in the region of Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both. If this had been the real Yugoslav People's Army wearing red stars on their caps, I wouldn't have been worried. But they had changed the insignia, and they did not hide the fact that it was a Chetnik army and that there was no place for Ustashas and balijas in the ranks of that army. And this is why the people protested, and this is why we wanted to find some way to protect them. And this was only the beginning. These manoeuvres took place, indeed, but other things happened after that, after the war in Slovenia, in Croatia, and later during the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina. But at that time, at the beginning, the idea was simply to protect the people, to avoid negative reaction, and also the possibility of their being killed by the ones who had issued the mobilisation call-up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And did you find ways, even perhaps if not effective on the long term, but did you find any solutions or did you propose any ways out of the situation you deemed to be not a good one?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: They came to my house, in particular when mobilising the youths, 18 or 19 years of age, and my personal advice to them was not to respond to the call-up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did you discuss these kind of matters with others, non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. Is there any need for further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Not from me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Loukas, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Just in relation to the questions that His Honour asked, Mr. Karabeg, you're aware that the JNA did not change their insignia? Are you aware when the JNA changed their insignia, firstly, as a general point?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Individuals did all kinds of things. If you had been in Sanski Most and seen that for yourself, you would have asked a different question. But I cannot give you a specific answer to your question because I really don't know when exactly they changed the insignia.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay. And now, I'm just wondering if you could tell me what law it is whereby the president of the Executive Board consents to JNA manoeuvres, if you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is this a question that arises from the questions from the Bench?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, everything is related to everything, but this is not a question that arises out of the questions of the Bench.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. I'll withdraw it.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Just in relation to the questions that His Honour asked you, you do, of course, recall giving evidence previously in the Brdjanin and Talic case. And you were asked about these particular JNA exercises. Do you recall being asked about that?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Your Honour, those particular portions are, of course, in evidence. Your Honours will recall they're at pages 6213 and 6214 where Mr. Karabeg has given some previous answers in relation to these particular military exercises. And I just propose to allow Mr. Karabeg the opportunity to confirm what he said in relation to those exercises at that point, arising from Your Honours' questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me just... Yes, the problem is how to deal with that. Are we going to read it to him or are we -- it is, of course, in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and I'm willing to agree that the transcript reflects he was asked those questions and he gave those answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He gave those answers. Is there any need -- he gave these answers under oath.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I note the time, and I would invite Your Honour to look at that particular segment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So that's, then, where the Prosecution agrees that this is a correct transcript of his testimony, you for that reason refrain from asking for confirmation, but at the same time, you have drawn the attention of the Chamber to this part of his evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. That's correct. There is one other aspect, Your Honour, this question about the diary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: When does the Bench propose to make a decision about that particular aspect? Because I think, from the Defence perspective, obviously if a diary exists, we would like to see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. If the Chamber would like to have it produced, then of course the parties would have a copy as well. And then of course, it would possibly raise an issue of any further examination in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the future.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. I would be seeking that diary. I place that on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You would like to see it anyhow. You invite the Chamber to ask the witness to produce that.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Precisely, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Karabeg, could you tell us where your diary is. Is it at home or is it with you in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At home, in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber gladly accepts your offer to give the original. I think once the parties have inspected the original, that it might be returned to you so that it's your diary. Ms. Loukas, I'm just wondering how to arrange this. Wouldn't it be the best way, since the witness is called by the Prosecution, that the witness -- that the Chamber calls upon the Prosecution to present the diary in evidence? That would save you the concerns about translations, et cetera. So that we ask the witness to give it to the Prosecution. Is it in a booklet or is it looseleaf, Mr. Karabeg? Or is it in a --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's in a bound notebook. I would have to give you the entire notebook, which otherwise contains the overall chronology of events and my notes. Because my note is only part of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Wouldn't it be a good procedure that we invite the witness to give this notebook, which is bound as far as I understand, to the Prosecution; that a first glance at the original will be cast on it by Prosecution and Defence in order to identify those parts that seem to be relevant. It might cover a period not relevant for this case. And that then the parties would agree on what parts to be translated in writing. Because I take it for a first impression, not everything has to be translated in full, and the Defence will certainly have an opportunity to look through it and see what's relevant and what's not relevant. And that it will then be produced. And whether this would be a reason to ask Mr. Karabeg to come back is a matter still to be determined once we have received the information.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Precisely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then that's the procedure. Mr. Karabeg, you'll hear from the Prosecution, someone will be in touch with you in order to organise how you would deliver your notebook to an investigator of the Prosecution. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I would. But I'm afraid that you misunderstood me. I will send you the original, the entire notebook, but I'm not willing to have the entire diary translated, only the portion relating to the notes concerning this meeting. There's no need to translate the entire diary. The rest has nothing to do with this. But there's only half a page of text which needs to be translated, which is relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What is relevant and what is not relevant is, of course, it could be some of the events -- because you gave a lot of information both in your statements and in your testimony, the period as such might be of importance. So of course, we are not going to translate any irrelevant parts. And as you may have noticed, that I would like to give an opportunity to the parties to identify what are the relevant parts, and of course this case is not about everything that happened in all periods of time but of course is concentrated on certain events. And of course, especially relevant might be those parts that reflect whatever is in your statements and what is in your testimony, that would be the most relevant part. It could be to see whether dates are correct, correctly stated, or... So I would like to invite you to -- and if you would like the -- if there's any disagreement between the parties about what is relevant and what is irrelevant, that the Chamber would intervene so in order not to reveal any of your personal matters without a clear function in seeking the truth. Would you agree with that? Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. If I may something before he answers, Your Honour. If he has some concerns about personal, private matters that are in his diary that he would not like to be shared with me or with the Defence counsel, perhaps he could indicate in some fashion where those portions are in his diary. We can give that to the Court first to make a determination about whether or not it was relevant or pertinent. And if not, we would never see it, only the Court would. Perhaps he would feel more comfortable with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, would that be a...?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Of course, the determination, of course, of what's relevant or not relevant is ultimately a matter for the Court. And I think that the Court would have to examine the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but of course the question is whether the first screening, if there are particular parts of which the witness would say this is purely private, that means concerns about the health of his children or, well, whatever, or whether he had a disagreement with a family member, these kind of things, so that they will not -- they will be protected because they could not play any role in what we are seeking, and we are seeking different things than the personal matters of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. There's no problem in relation to something that is purely personal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Karabeg, I discussed now with the parties how we could protect your personal life and nevertheless have a more ample opportunity to take advantage of the fact that you have written down notes at the time of the events you are -- you testified about or you gave statements about. Would you agree with that procedure so that you can indicate "Please do not touch this and this and this part." That would not come to the parties but first go to the Chamber so that we can identify that it's really irrelevant and what might be relevant.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. I agree. But that was not the initial idea of my suggestion. I just wanted to offer you this as proof that I made a note of that meeting in Banja Luka. Now you have expanded it to something else. Of course, I will provide the entire notebook, and I'm prepared to accept your suggestion. I will circle what I consider to be private and wish to remain secret.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you would do that, the Chamber is very grateful with your cooperation to allow us to seek the truth as good as we can, assisted by the parties. In some systems, one would say to find the truth rather than to seek the truth, but that's...

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just before you finally end on that question, I think there was just a matter that my case manager wanted to clarify in relation to the particular reading out of that last exhibit. And I think it might be appropriate to deal with that at some stage. I just thought I would put that on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Reading out the last exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: That's the caption related to the photograph, Your Honour. That's D14.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it's just that -- I think there was a slight nuance in the translation that my case manager is just explaining to me. But I think it's best if Ms. Cmeric explains that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course. I asked specific attention of the interpreters for specifically this, whether if there would be any need to come back to that, then perhaps it becomes very technical. So then perhaps you could write it down in a few lines and say this is the original text, it has been translated by the interpreters first as the meeting of the Municipal Assembly. Then in my -- then you gave a slightly different translation of it, so that --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I might just get Ms. Cmeric to explain to you what the actual issue is because I think it's better cleared up now than later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If Ms. Cmeric could enlighten us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, do we need to do this with the witness still here? If not, perhaps we can let him go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would it raise any further issues to be put to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I tend to think not, Your Honour. It's a very subtle difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it, Mr. Karabeg, that you'll not leave The Hague within one hour. So if there would be an urgent need to have you back in court, you'll hear from us. But we do not expect that. I'd first like to thank you very much for the evidence you've given. You've answered a lot of questions by both parties and by the Bench. Thank you very much also for your full cooperation in providing your notes to this Chamber. And I wish you a safe trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Your Honours, I should also like to thank you on these fair proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karabeg.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Cmeric, I suggest that we do it after the break. We adjourn until 5 minutes to 1.00. And is the Prosecution then ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We are, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Cmeric, could you tell us what you have in your mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. CMERIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. It's just on the page 40, and I believe it's the end of page 40 and very beginning of page 41. In response to your question, I believe that I made a slip of the tongue, saying that it was a ceremonial session held in the Municipal Assembly. And I believe that created a slight misunderstanding. So the fact is it's not about the translation of the article of the actual language of the article, it's just that it is -- it was actually a ceremonial session of the Municipal Assembly, but held in the cultural centre in Banja Luka, in the cultural centre hall. And for that, I apologise to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That also casts another light on the answer of the witness whether he would recognise this hall. He says, well, I have been there, but it seems different to me. But apart from that, you have put some questions, Ms. Loukas, in relation to this meeting, and especially who was on the front row, apart from whether we can see everyone in the front row. But the Chamber also wondered whether there is one front row of approximately ten chairs or whether there are two front rows. If the -- we cannot see on this photograph whether on the left-hand side of the photograph there's a path in the middle of the hall or whether it's just the... And even that would leave open other questions like whether this was the meeting or it was at the same time and whether people ever moved from the first row to other rows. Well, a lot of questions. But specifically, the question on if this is the hall of the cultural centre, whether this is ten chairs wide or two times ten chairs, that's an issue the Chamber would very much like to be informed about. Also, in order to better be able to evaluate the testimony of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Your Honour. And of course that photograph indeed only arrived just prior to us coming into Court. But of course, we'll be calling further evidence in relation to that ultimately, of course, in the Defence case. But if we can get any more clarity in relation to that question prior to that, Your Honour, we will be informing the Trial Chamber as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. I thank you for your explanation, Ms. Cmeric.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is one further matter. There's obviously one outstanding matter in terms of material to be tendered in respect of this witness and of course in respect to Sanski Most overall, and that's this Rule 68 material in relation to the witness Mr. Adil Draganovic. And of course that material incorporates that statement that Your Honour was asking about as well. And I think that we could probably get that together probably not today, because we'll need to print out that material, but possibly tomorrow I would have thought.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand you well that you say you'd rather have this material tendered until now all in the same context of Sanski Most, because we had some problems of authenticity of some documents were concerned. We had another document where at least the Chamber didn't know where it came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I know there was a Defence objection to, I think, item number 111, P111, and I think P113. And Your Honour had asked, I think, for some additional information, and I advised the Court yesterday that the information I had was our internal documentation showed it had been received from AID in November 1995. I have been unable to learn that there's any additional information about where those documents were between the date on the document, June 1992, and November 1995. However, in the testimony -- yes, the 92 bis (D) statements of Adil Draganovic and in the testimony of three other witnesses who are sensitive sources who testified in the Brdjanin/Talic case who were also listed as witnesses in this case and of whom I think two if not three will be testifying in this case, talk about that specific document. And Mr. Draganovic talks in some detail about the whole collection of documents from Sanski Most that he found and turned over to AID and some that he turned over directly to the OTP. Your Honour, so with that in mind, I know the Court would perhaps like to have some additional information, but we would like to tender Exhibits 98 through 115 at this time with whatever reservations the Court has about any of those specific items.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber finds it appropriate to delay the decision. That would not be necessary for all of the exhibits as a matter of fact, because some of them seem to be very unproblematic. But in order not to lose one or two out of sight, we would rather deal with all of them perhaps at the end of Sanski Most or at any appropriate moment when we have sufficient information to give proper decisions on it. If the parties would agree with that, but even if they would not agree with that, I'd like to ask the usher to escort the next witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, while that's being done, I'll just quickly use up the time, if I may. Your Honour asked for a reference to the evidence-in-chief in relation to the question of those two villages Vrhpolje and Hrustovo. And, Your Honour, that particular reference is page 6159 in the evidence-in-chief. And of course, that will have to -- that page or perhaps the surrounding pages will have to form part of the exhibits for this particular segment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If then both parties, where reference is made to the examination-in-chief, could tender the relevant pages so that we have them all, of course we could find them elsewhere, but that's not the way of doing it. If you would provide the Chamber with the relevant pages.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The next witness, as far as I understand, there are no protective measures in effect, Mr. Resch? And it would be Mr. Rajif Begic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Begic, as I understand. Mr. Begic, before --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- giving evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration of which the text has been handed out to you now by the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Begic. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You will first be examined by counsel for the Prosecution, Mr. Resch. Mr. Resch, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Could you please tell us your name.

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: My name is Rajif Begic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Mr. Begic, when were you born?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 23rd of September, 1967.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Where were you born, Mr. Begic?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: I was born in Klijevci, near Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Where have you lived between when you were born and 1992?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: I lived in the village of Begici near Sanski Most, and I went to four years of primary school in Klijevci and another four years in Tomina, and then I did my vocational training in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to have the first map given an exhibit number and shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, of course, we still expect a few other exhibits in relation to the witness we had, but I think we just continue the numbering now. And Madam Registrar, what would be the next number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The next number, I believe, is P115.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I hope this document can be available on the computer monitors through the Sanction programme.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think that depends on your -- yes, we have got it on our screen at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Mr. Begic, you said you lived in the village of Begici. Do we see that near the bottom of the map, the south end of Sanski Most, the direction of Kljuc? Just above Vrhpolje?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes, by Vrhpolje, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: You said you also -- you were born in the village of Klijevci, which is also just to the northwest of Begici?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: Begici and Kenjari belongs to Klijevci. It is within the composition of the village of Klijevci and the village is Begici. So when it is listed in documents, they list the main place, Klijevci and not Begici.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. And just so everyone is clear, you previously testified before this Tribunal in May of 2002 in the Brdjanin and Talic trial, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: We'll be covering a number of those same events, but it's important that we talk about them in full so this Chamber can also know of the events that you are here to testify about. I'd like to first talk about May of 1992 in Sanski Most. At that time, you were living in the hamlet of Begici, which is part of the settlement or village of Klijevci. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Thank you. You'll need to make an audible response for the record.

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: What was the ethnic background or make-up of most of the population of Begici?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: In the hamlet of Begici, in fact, in the village of Klijevci, looking from Sanski Most, the Sanski Most direction, Klijevci, as on the photograph, are most inhabited by Serbs. Then next to us is the Kenjari hamlet, which was inhabited by the Muslims. And right next to us was the hamlet of Stojanovici with a Serb population. And then the Begici hamlet once again was Muslim populated. So it was intermittent, Serb, Muslim, and mixed. Several houses were Croatian households towards Kasapnica, to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Hrustovo and Vrhpolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: I forgot to ask earlier, but what is your nationality, sir?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: I'm a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: In May of 1992, did you observe soldiers patrolling in the area around your village?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Could you tell us about what you saw, what -- who were these soldiers?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: Next to us, the first hamlet, Stojanovici, a Serb hamlet, they had a checkpoint on the main road leading to Kenjari. And at that checkpoint, there were our Serb neighbours. It was manned by Serb neighbours dressed in army uniforms. And -- but nothing important happened at that checkpoint, nothing of significance. But if somebody tried to pass by that way, they would stop them, search the vehicle or tractor or whatever you were driving through. And we knew that in Klijevci, in the four-year primary school was the location of a unit by a man called Mijatovic who was the leader there of that group. And he came to visit our hamlet on one occasion with two or three soldiers, accompanied by two or three soldiers, just to see the lie of the land. And we learned from him that that's how things stood.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Was that Mijatovic, was he a Serb?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Do you know if he was a member of any particular military unit?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: Well, I really can't say. I think it was all the 6th Krajina group throughout that territory. Now, whether that unit had a special name, I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Do you know who the commander of the 6th Krajina Brigade was in May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes. The commander was Commander Branko Basara.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could have the next map, it's the Hrustovo-Vrhpolje overview map, given an identification number and placed in front of the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, this map will be marked P116.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We just had 116. Would it not then be 117 now?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. P117.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From what I see on my screen, Mr. Resch, I do not know what questions are there to come, but we had -- well, it's a procedural incident. If we could just stop for one second. We had a procedural incident where a witness was asked about certain features in the area, and they -- one second, Mr. Usher. We had an incident where the Defence complained about the answer being shown on eight small pictures close to a map. I don't know what your questions will be, but if you would like to -- for example, to ask him which were the houses of the eight richest people in the area and you would show eight houses that by any chance would be in the possession of the most rich people in that area, then the -- I could expect a similar objection from the Defence. And as I -- as the Chamber decided before, that would not be the proper way of doing it. So I've got no idea what you were going to ask the witness, but if the answer you expect would be the same as we see on eight small pictures, then I'd rather you to ask the question without showing these pictures to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will be asking questions about two of the eight pictures. And I have a blowup of one of the eight. But I don't think the questions are in the same vein as yesterday, and they're not necessarily going to be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're not going to ask -- to identify, to say, for example, do you know any grocery shops, and there would be two grocery shops on this picture? Then I would like you to ask could you tell us where the grocery shops in the village were, and then later on you could ask confirmation on whether what the witness answered is shown on this picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: I don't think they're as -- the photographs and the map is not as suggestive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. You're sufficiently warned now, I would say. So please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: If the witness could also have a pen because I will be asking him to make some marks on this map eventually.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Exhibit P117 is an overview map of a portion of Sanski Most, the southern middle region of Sanski Most, if I can characterise it that way, showing a close-up view of the area between Klijevci and Vrhpolje, which we'll be discussing during the testimony. During May of 1992, do you recall any radio broadcasts regarding calls for turning in weapons in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: There were calls like that prior to the events themselves, which took place on the 31st of May, just before those events. But over a long period of time, no, I know that it happened very briefly before the events themselves that such calls did exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Were these calls to turn in arms directed at any one national group or the other?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Through the radio, over the radio, Sanski Most Radio, the population, whole population, was informed of this. Hrustovo, Vrhpolje, Klijevci, and all the others, to surrender their weapons, to hand them in to the nearest Serbian checkpoint, the closest checkpoint to them. So appeals of that kind were made over the radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: And did you or anyone from your village turn in any weapons?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: What sort of weapons did you turn in?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: The weapons we had in our village that we knew about, that had been there for many years before that, we handed in those weapons. And I know exactly who had what and who turned in what. At our checkpoint, our neighbours went to the checkpoint who had weapons and handed them over. They were Muhamed Bilic. He had an old hunting rifle. It was of the Zastava trademark. It was a very old rifle. And then Begic Hadija had a 9-millimetre pistol, and we all knew about that because it was registered regularly. And Kula Ismet handed over a pistol belonging to his brother-in-law, Hadzic Musta, who was not there. He was working in Slovenia during that period and his wife gave her brother the pistol to hand it over in their names so they wouldn't have any problems being in possession of such a weapon. Midhet Ceric, or Enes, they handed over a pistol, too. I don't know what the brand of that was or what the calibre was, but I do know that those four weapons were handed over to the Serbs who were manning the checkpoint closest to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Do you know if your -- any of your Serb neighbours turned in weapons to these checkpoints in response to these calls for turning in weapons?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: I don't understand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Were you aware of any of your Serb neighbours turning in weapons in response to these calls?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: No. They still -- they were still in possession of those weapons. And it wasn't stated that the Serb population should hand in their weapons. This just applied to the Muslims. They were told to hand in their weapons. So I didn't see any of the Serbs hand in their weapons, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: I'd like now to move to the 25th of May, 1992. Do you recall soldiers entering your village on the 25th of May?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall that. They entered the villages around noon. They came to our hamlet of Donji Begici. And during those few seconds, or a few seconds before that, two small boys warned me that the soldiers were coming and that I should take refuge, take shelter. So I hid by the river several hundreds metres away from my house where I could observe what was going on from that vantage point, see what was happening in our hamlet.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Were you by yourself?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: No. I was with my younger brother and uncle Munib when we hid from the soldiers. Or cousin, with my cousin.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: What was your brother's name?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: His name was Nedzad Begic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: How old was he in 1992?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: He was 18 at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: And your cousin, I didn't catch his name. How old was he and what was his first name?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: At the time, he was 26. And his name was Munib Begic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Were you able to see what the soldiers did when they entered Begici?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes. They entered into the -- entered the hamlet of Gornji Begici and Donji Begici at the same time. I couldn't see what was going on up there in Gornji Begici but I learned about it later on, whereas they entered Donji Begici and maltreated the people. They beat my mother, for example, and two other elderly persons, Huse and Radojka Begic, and they intimidated the population generally, the population that they had collected together in a garage, and some people shouted out, Beat them, set fire to the houses, and things like that. And then a soldier, Dusko Savic, who went to school with me for a few years, four years of elementary school, he beat up my mother and took all her gold jewellery away from her and all her money. So there was a lot of provocation like that, and after that event, they withdrew towards the checkpoint at Stojanovici. And they also killed my dog on the occasion.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: A moment ago it was cousin, not uncle.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: These soldiers who entered Begici on the 25th of May, do you know what unit they were from or what their ethnicity was?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: They were Serb soldiers. And the unit, those who already lived in Klijevci, or rather were in Klijevci, Mijatovici. However, in Gornji Begici, it was the Serbs, the neighbouring Serbs living next to our hamlet who entered that hamlet. Cosic, Ranko Cosic and his men. So they entered Gornji Begici, the upper hamlet, and behaved like that and had control over the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: What were these soldiers wearing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Resch, we heard as the evidence of this witness that "I couldn't see what was going on there in Gornji Begici." And then later on he testified of what happened in a garage when he was supposed to be at a distance of a couple of hundred metres. And now you're asking further questions on what happened in Gornji Begici. He described they behaved like that and had control of the area. Could you try to find out more specifically what is the personal observation of the witness and what is hearsay and what's then the source of what he learned. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Is it fair to say Begici is divided into two halves; Gornji Begici and Donji Begici?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I've already said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: And from where you and your brother and cousin were hiding, would you -- which Begici could you observe?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: Donji Begici. We could observe several houses located next to the Sana. We could also see many soldiers. We could hear shouts. We could hear people moan as they were being beaten. We could distinctly hear all of their voices, plus what I learned afterwards from my mother. And I also learned who was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: So you learned from your mother about the events that day in Gornji Begici. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Also, what happened in Gornji Begici, because they went to Gornji Begici and learned from the locals there what had happened to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: The soldiers who were in Donji Begici, could you recognise some of them?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: I couldn't, but when my mother told me that it was Dusko Savic, I believed her because we all knew each other because we went to school together. She recognised others as well, but she couldn't be bothered to tell me all of their names. But she identified him because she had had contacts with his mother and he went to the nearby school. It is all a very small area. The village of Klijevci is not far away and we basically know each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Were any houses destroyed on the 25th of May?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: Not at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: What about property? Was any property taken from any people, as far as you either saw or were told?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Some took cars. Some took tractors. They said that this property was being commandeered for the needs of the military. We didn't say anything against that. Mustafic's car, for instance, was taken away. We didn't pay much attention to that. But I know that as far as my mother's is concerned, her gold jewellery and money was taken away. I don't know about others, so I cannot testify about that. On that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Let's move to the 31st of May, 1992. Did you hear any radio broadcasts on that day about military events in the area?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: No. Nothing was broadcast over the radio, nothing concerning the events that were to take place. I don't even know whether we had electricity in those days. I cannot remember. But as far as I recall, nothing was broadcast. Nothing major, at any rate.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Did you see any soldiers or did any soldiers arrive in Begici on the 31st of May?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the 31st of May in the afternoon, from the direction of Dizdarevici, the area where several houses are located right next to the road, they started with those houses. They rounded up the populations there and told them to go in the direction of Donji Begici. And when they got to where we were, they told us to come out and to go, all of us, to Gornji Begici. There were many soldiers around on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Do you know what unit these soldiers were from?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: No. I don't know which particular unit they belonged to, but I think that they were all members of that unit which was located in the school in Klijevci.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: That was the unit of the 6th Krajina Brigade in Klijevci?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, of course, because the 6th Krajina Brigade had a wider area of responsibility which included not only Klijevci, but Sanski Most and its surroundings. So that's why I think that all of these events were happening in the area which was under the control of the 6th Krajina Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: To be clear, these soldiers who showed up on the 31st of May, were they Serbs?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Did you recognise any of them or know any of them?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I knew them. Apart from our next-door neighbours, I also knew several young men who lived in Sanski Most. Some I knew by sight; some I'd gone to school with or socialised with at the time I was an apprentice, so I know that they were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: You were saying the soldiers told everyone to go to Gornji Begici. Is that what happened?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's what we did. We helped some elderly people, and we went to Gornji Begici, all of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Were these soldiers armed?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: Of course they were armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Did you feel you had any choice but to follow their orders or instructions?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. We didn't even try to look for an option, for an alternative because they had expressly told us not to move too far away from our homes, both in Gornji Begici and Donji Begici. So when they -- it was on that first occasion when they arrived that they told the population to stick together until further notice. And that's why I decided when I got home not to move around too much, not to leave the area. I was just prepared to meet my fate.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Just in relation to that, Your Honour, the -- I'm loath to constantly object, but Your Honour's injunction about ensuring that what information is personal observation of the witness and what is perhaps hearsay, particularly when we have a reference to an answer that includes Donji Begici and Gornji Begici, perhaps those sort of matters could be cleared up by the Prosecution. That answer does seem to interpolate both personal observation and hearsay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Resch, if you could keep that in mind. Although it's here, it seems to be a bit less disturbing than it was when I made the intervention. Please proceed. And may I ask your attention also for the clock and to find a suitable moment to stop within, well, let's say, the next three minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: I've got a point in mind, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: When the soldiers told you to head towards Gornji Begici, were you with any of your family members?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes, we were all together at that moment. Donji Begici consisted of five houses, and the population of those five households were all together. And we went to Gornji Begici together, all of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Which family members were with you?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: At that time, my mother was there and my two younger brothers.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Maybe this would help clear up some of the confusion: How far is Gornji Begici from Donji Begici?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: Several hundred metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: What happened when you got to Gornji Begici?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: When we arrived in Gornji Begici, we realised that the soldiers had already taken possession of the village. They were already deployed along the road. And we could see from Safet Begic's basement that the villagers of Gornji Begici were coming out. Apparently, they had been ordered to remain in the basement throughout that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's about as convenient a spot as any.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Begic, we'll stop for today. We would like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.00, as far as I'm aware of in the same courtroom. Madam Registrar, I think, the same courtroom. And I'd like to instruct you not to speak with anyone; not with Defence, not with Prosecution, no one, about the testimony you have given or the testimony you expect to give tomorrow. So no conversations about your testimony with anyone. We'll adjourn until tomorrow morning, 9.00, same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 27th day of May, 2004, at 9.00 a.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
